claims.text: Wear resistance in FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings during high-temperature sliding is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale oxide phases.
Microscopic deformation in FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings during high-temperature sliding is primarily governed by the stability and distribution of nanoscale oxide phases.
Increasing copper content alters the oxide-phase composition and distribution in the coating.
Increasing copper content reduces wear resistance because it produces less stable oxide phases.
Increasing copper content increases microscopic deformation because it produces less stable oxide phases.
The baseline coating has a uniform microstructure and a typical oxide-phase distribution.
Nanoscale oxide phases form within or on the HEA coating during high-temperature exposure.
Copper enrichment disrupts the formation of stable protective oxides such as Cr2O3 or NiO.
Copper enrichment produces oxide layers that are less uniform and less adherent.
Less uniform and less adherent oxide layers cause increased local softening.
Local softening accelerates wear and deformation under sliding.
Increasing copper content will increase the wear rate during high-temperature sliding.
Increasing copper content will increase plastic deformation, including greater plasticity, deeper grooves, or deeper wear tracks.
The baseline coating exhibits stable oxide-phase formation and moderate wear resistance.
The predicted effects apply above 500 degrees Celsius in air for thin FeNiCrCoCu coatings on conventional metal substrates.
The effects may differ at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres.
The expected effect size is moderate.
